title: Socratic Mind: Impact of a Novel GenAI-Powered Assessment Tool on Student Learning and Higher-Order Thinking
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a generative AI-powered formative assessment tool, Socratic Mind, can improve student engagement, learning outcomes, and higher-order thinking in higher education. The authors focus on a key concern in AI-supported education: many AI tools support lower-level recall or procedural tasks but do not effectively foster deeper reasoning, reflection, and critical thinking. The study asks how students engage with the tool, whether user experience influences engagement, whether the tool improves perceived and actual learning outcomes, and how it affects higher-order thinking skills such as problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-reflection.

The intervention studied is Socratic Mind, a GenAI-based assessment system that conducts adaptive Socratic dialogue with students through spoken or written responses. Instructors configure opening prompts, desired answers, rubrics, and misconceptions, and the system follows up with personalized questions until conceptual clarity is reached. The tool was used as an optional extra-credit assignment aligned with course quiz content. The study used a quasi-experimental mixed-methods approach, combining system logs, surveys on engagement and user experience, academic performance data, and thematic analysis of open-ended student reflections. Quantitative analyses included regression and difference-in-differences models.

The population consisted of undergraduate students enrolled in a 16-week fully online asynchronous introductory computing course (CS1301) at a U.S. research university. The final analytic sample included 171 students who completed the AI assignment and post-survey on time, drawn from a larger course enrollment of 579 students. Students were assigned to complete the AI-based assignment for either Unit 3 or Unit 4, creating a comparison structure across different course units. The context was a large-scale online course delivered through Canvas and edX.

The main findings show that students reported high affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement with the tool, and these engagement levels were positively associated with usability, perceived effectiveness, and satisfaction. Students who used the tool showed a significantly smaller decline in quiz performance over time compared with peers, with especially strong benefits for lower-performing students, though similar effects were not found for unit tests. Qualitative responses suggested perceived gains in problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-reflection, with weaker effects for verbal communication due in part to limited use of audio interaction. Overall, the paper concludes that AI-mediated Socratic dialogue is a promising scalable formative assessment strategy for supporting engagement and higher-order thinking in online undergraduate learning.

identified_tools.name: Socratic Mind
identified_tools.description: A GenAI-powered formative assessment tool that simulates Socratic dialogue through adaptive questioning, allowing students to respond by text or speech and providing immediate personalized feedback. Instructors configure prompts, desired answers, rubrics, and misconceptions, and the system can assist with question design from uploaded course materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an optional extra-credit AI-based assessment in a large online introductory computing course, where students completed Unit 3 or Unit 4 assignments aligned to quiz topics and engaged in adaptive Socratic questioning about programming concepts, debugging, and real-world applications.

findings.finding_summary: Using a difference-in-differences regression on quiz performance, students who participated in the Socratic Mind assignment showed a significantly smaller decline in quiz scores over time than peers who did not use the tool. Overall post scores declined by about 11.84 points, but the treatment group’s drop was reduced by an estimated 3.30 points (Post*Treatment: B = 3.300, SE = 1.373, b2 = .107, p < .05); the final analyzed sample was 171 students, though the regression used 798 score observations.
findings.measure: Course quiz scores over time (difference-in-differences regression comparing pre- and post-assignment quiz performance)

findings.finding_summary: The same difference-in-differences analysis found no significant treatment effect on unit test scores. The interaction term for tests was not significant (Post*Treatment: B = -3.017, SE = 2.631, b2 = -.053, p > .05), indicating no detectable buffering effect on the more open-ended programming tests.
findings.measure: Course test scores over time (difference-in-differences regression comparing pre- and post-assignment test performance)

findings.finding_summary: An extended quiz regression suggested the tool particularly benefited lower-performing students. For every 1-point lower baseline score, the benefit of the tool increased by about 0.21 points (Pre*Treatment: B = -0.217, SE = 0.104, b2 = -.635, p < .05), alongside a significant positive post-treatment interaction (Post*Treatment: B = 22.764, SE = 9.393, b2 = .736, p < .05).
findings.measure: Moderation of quiz-score treatment effects by pre-intervention quiz performance
findings.effect_size: Pre*Treatment: B=-0.217, b2=-.635, p<.05; Post*Treatment: B=22.764, b2=.736, p<.05

findings.finding_summary: Thematic analysis of 141 open-ended responses found that 69% of respondents reported positive changes in problem-solving after using Socratic Mind, often citing more structured step-by-step reasoning, deeper conceptual understanding, and greater confidence in debugging. About 17% reported no change and 12% reported mixed change.
findings.measure: Student reflections on problem-solving skill development

findings.finding_summary: In qualitative responses, 62% of respondents reported positive changes in critical thinking, describing stronger analytical thinking, clearer reasoning, and better evaluation of coding logic from multiple perspectives. By contrast, 31% reported no change and 5% reported mixed experiences.
findings.measure: Student reflections on critical thinking skill development

findings.finding_summary: For self-reflection, 60% of respondents reported gains after interacting with the tool, including more deliberate evaluation of their understanding and more intentional metacognitive behaviors. Meanwhile, 34% reported no change and about 1% reported mixed effects.
findings.measure: Student reflections on self-reflection/metacognitive skill development

findings.finding_summary: Perceived effects on verbal communication were more limited: 38% of respondents reported positive changes, while 56% reported no change, largely because many students typed rather than used the verbal interaction feature. Another 5% reported mixed experiences.
findings.measure: Student reflections on verbal communication skill development

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with a named intervention, comparison groups, and difference-in-differences analysis, which is stronger than correlational work but does not meet the standard of a fully rigorous RCT. The authors also note limits including single-course context and potential unmeasured confounding.
impact_tier_rationale: The clearest quantified academic effect is a modest positive buffering effect on quiz-score decline (B = 3.300; b2 = .107), with stronger benefits for lower-performing students, while test-score effects were null. Overall impact is positive but moderate and somewhat outcome-specific.
